what_it_does: Personalizing a pre-trained AI model on a small device — updating it with a user's own data so it adapts to them — normally requires running backpropagation, the mathematical process that figures out how to nudge every weight in the network to reduce errors. On a tiny microcontroller with less than 1 MB of working memory (RAM) and 2 MB of storage (flash), this is prohibitively expensive because each layer's intermediate activations must be kept in memory simultaneously. TinyMP tackles this with two complementary tricks. First, Gradient Condensing simplifies the structure of the gradient maps — the arrays of correction signals flowing backward through the network — so they take far less memory without hurting accuracy much. Second, Alternant Partial Update avoids updating all layers at once: instead it rotates through small subsets of parameters in alternating rounds, cutting the computation per step, and it does this without any offline search to figure out which parameters matter. Together the two techniques aim to make on-device personalization feasible on hardware that previously could not support any training at all. Quantitative results are from the abstract and should be confirmed in the full paper.
